title: Patient rights, nearest relative, IMHA and tribunals
blurb: Give s132 rights properly, identify the nearest relative, explain IMHA eligibility and tribunal windows.
question: Priya, 31, was detained under section 2 yesterday. She is distressed and says she did not take in what the nurse told her on admission. She is unmarried and lives with her partner of 2 years; her mother lives nearby. What should her nurse do, and who is her nearest relative?

teach.h: Rights are part of the treatment
teach.body: Detention removes liberty, so the Act builds in rights: to be told what is happening (s132), to have a nearest relative with protective powers (s26), to an independent mental health advocate (IMHA, s130A), and to challenge detention at the First-tier Tribunal (s66) or a managers' hearing. In plain English: nobody should be detained without knowing why, who can help them, and how to challenge it.

items: As soon as practicable after detention starts, help the patient understand which section they are held under and its effect.
Explain their right to apply to the tribunal, and the effect of other rights such as consent to treatment and discharge.
Give the information both orally AND in writing (s132(3)).
Send a copy to the nearest relative unless the patient objects (s132(4)).
If the patient does not understand, record it and try again; repeat rights at intervals.

steps.sub: Discharge blocked; no new order for 6 months

Qualifying informal patients: anyone discussing s57 treatment, and under-18s discussing s58A treatment such as ECT.

teach.body: Priya did not understand her rights, so the nurse repeats them calmly, orally and in writing, checks her understanding and records it. She is on s2, so she has 14 days from admission to apply to the tribunal, and she qualifies for an IMHA. She is unmarried, so her partner of 2 years counts as a spouse (cohabiting 6 months or more, s26(6)), so he is her nearest relative, ahead of her mother. A copy of the written information goes to him unless Priya objects.

teach.text: Under the 1983 Act the patient does NOT choose their nearest relative: it is set by the s26 list. An unsuitable NR can be displaced by the county court (s29). The patient-chosen 'nominated person' belongs to the Mental Health Act 2025, which is not yet in force.

items: s132: as soon as practicable, orally and in writing; copy to the NR unless the patient objects.
NR: first in the s26 list, with priority for a relative who lives with or cares for the patient.
NR discharge needs 72 hours' notice; an RC barring report blocks it and bars another order for 6 months.
Tribunal: s2 within 14 days; s3 and CTO once in the first 6 months; automatic referral if none.

summary: You can now give s132 rights correctly, identify the nearest relative from the s26 list, explain IMHA eligibility and state the tribunal application windows and automatic referrals. You can also describe how a nearest relative's discharge order can be barred.

A.q: How must information under section 132 be given to a detained patient?
options: Orally, at the first ward round
In writing to the nearest relative
A.why: Section 132(3): the steps taken must include giving the information both orally and in writing.

whyNot.0: Written information alone does not meet s132(3), and no signature is required by the Act.
whyNot.1: Oral information alone is not enough, and it should be given as soon as practicable.
whyNot.3: The NR receives a copy unless the patient objects; the duty is to the patient.

A.q: Within what period can a patient detained under section 2 apply to the tribunal?
A.why: Section 66(2)(a): within 14 days beginning with the day of admission.

whyNot.1: 28 days is the length of s2, and the NR's window after a barring report.
whyNot.2: 72 hours is the NR's notice period for discharge.
whyNot.3: 6 months is the s3 and CTO application window.

A.q: How much notice must a nearest relative give hospital managers before discharging a detained patient?
A.why: Section 25(1): at least 72 hours' notice in writing, during which the RC can issue a barring report.

whyNot.1: 7 days is the longer-term s17 leave threshold.
whyNot.2: 14 days is the s2 tribunal application window.

B.q: Mr Novak, 48, is permanently separated from his wife by agreement and lives with and is cared for by his younger sister. His adult son lives abroad and is not ordinarily resident in the UK. Who is his nearest relative?
B.why: A relative who lives with or cares for the patient takes priority (s26). A separated spouse does not count, and a relative not ordinarily resident in the UK is disregarded.

whyNot.0: A spouse permanently separated by agreement is treated as if dead for this purpose (s26(5)(b)).
whyNot.1: The carer sister takes priority over relatives higher in the list, including his mother.
whyNot.2: A relative not ordinarily resident in the UK is treated as if dead (s26(5)(a)).

B.q: Which patient is NOT a qualifying patient for an IMHA?
options: A patient on a community treatment order
B.why: Section 130C(2)(a) excludes patients held under s4, s5(2), s5(4), s135 and s136.

B.q: A nearest relative orders a patient's discharge from section 3. The RC reports that the patient would be likely to act dangerously if discharged. What follows?
options: The patient is discharged after 72 hours
The NR may apply to the tribunal within 28 days
The NR may order discharge again in 1 month
The managers must hold a hearing within 7 days of notice
B.why: The barring report makes the order ineffective and bars another for 6 months (s25); for a s3 patient the NR may apply to the tribunal within 28 days of being told (s66).

whyNot.0: The barring report stops the discharge.
whyNot.2: No further NR discharge order may be made for 6 months.
whyNot.3: The Act does not set a 7-day managers' hearing requirement here.

C.q: Priya, on section 2, did not understand her rights when told on admission because she was very distressed. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
options: Record that rights were given on admission
Ask her nearest relative to explain them to her later
Wait for the tribunal hearing to explain them
Repeat them orally and in writing, and record it
C.why: Section 132 requires practicable steps to ensure the patient understands; if she did not, the information should be repeated orally and in writing and the attempts recorded.

whyNot.0: The duty is to take steps to ensure she understands, not just to give the information once.
whyNot.1: The NR receives a copy but the duty to the patient stays with the hospital.
whyNot.2: Her tribunal window is 14 days, so waiting could cost her the right to apply.

C.q: Tom, 17, has been detained under section 3 for 20 months. His only tribunal hearing was held 5 months into his detention, and he has not applied since. What must the hospital managers do?
options: Refer his case to the tribunal now
Wait until 3 years since his last hearing
Hold a managers' hearing in place of a tribunal
C.why: Section 68(6): managers must refer if more than 1 year has passed since the last tribunal for a patient under 18 (3 years for adults).

whyNot.1: Three years is the adult period; under-18s are referred after 1 year.
whyNot.2: The duty depends on time since the last hearing, not his birthday.
whyNot.3: A managers' hearing does not replace the statutory tribunal referral.

C.q: Aisha, an informal 16-year-old in-patient, is discussing ECT with her consultant. Her mother asks if Aisha can have an independent advocate. What is the position?
options: No, as IMHAs are for detained patients
Yes, if the tribunal appoints one
Yes, she is a qualifying patient
C.why: Section 130C(3)(b): an informal patient under 18 who discusses s58A treatment (ECT) with a doctor or AC is a qualifying patient.

whyNot.0: Some informal patients qualify, including under-18s discussing ECT.
whyNot.1: Being under 18 is part of what makes her qualify here.
whyNot.2: IMHA services are arranged by the local authority, not appointed by the tribunal.

reteach.title: Tell, protect, challenge
reteach.question: What three things does the Act guarantee a detained patient?

blocks.body: TELL: s132 rights, orally and in writing, repeated until understood. PROTECT: a nearest relative from the s26 list with powers to be informed, object to s3 and seek discharge, plus an IMHA for most detained and CTO patients. CHALLENGE: tribunal applications within set windows, automatic referrals if none, and managers' hearings.

blocks.text: Patients on s4, s5(2), s5(4), s135 and s136 do not qualify for an IMHA; most other detained patients do.

explain.body: Managers must take practicable steps, as soon as practicable, to make sure the patient understands their section, its effect and their tribunal rights, orally and in writing, with a copy to the NR unless the patient objects.

test.q: When can the hospital withhold a copy of the written section 132 information from the nearest relative?
options: When the RC disagrees with the NR
When the patient is on section 2
test.why: Section 132(4): the NR is sent a copy except where the patient otherwise requests.

whyNot.0: Age is not the exception in s132(4).
whyNot.2: The RC's view is not the test.
whyNot.3: The duty applies to s2 patients as well.

explain.body: The first person in the s26 list, with priority for a relative who lives with or cares for the patient. Cohabitees of 6 months count as spouses; non-relatives after 5 years come last. The patient does not choose.

test.q: Which relative is chosen first when two are in the same rank of the s26 list?
options: The one living nearest to the hospital site
The elder, whole blood before half blood
The one chosen by the AMHP
test.why: Section 26(3)-(4): whole blood relatives are preferred to half blood, then the elder, unless one lives with or cares for the patient.

whyNot.0: The patient cannot choose under the 1983 Act.
whyNot.1: Distance from the hospital is not a factor.
whyNot.3: The AMHP identifies the NR by the statutory rules, not by choice.

explain.body: Local authorities must arrange independent mental health advocates. Qualifying: most detained patients (not s4, s5, s135, s136), CTO and guardianship patients, and some informal patients considering s57 or (under 18) ECT.

test.q: Who must arrange IMHA services in England?
test.why: Section 130A: the local social services authority must make arrangements for IMHAs.

whyNot.0: Managers must tell patients about IMHAs, but the local authority arranges them.
whyNot.2: The CQC monitors use of the Act; it does not arrange advocacy.
whyNot.3: The tribunal hears applications; it does not arrange advocacy.

explain.body: s2: apply within 14 days. s3 and CTO: once in the first 6 months, then once per renewal period. Managers must refer at 6 months if no application or reference has been made, and when more than 3 years have passed since the last tribunal (1 year if under 18).

test.q: A section 3 patient has not applied to the tribunal by the end of 6 months. What must happen?
options: The right to a tribunal is lost
The NR must apply on their behalf
test.why: Section 68(1)-(2): managers must refer the case to the tribunal at the end of 6 months if no application or reference has been made.

whyNot.1: The automatic referral protects the patient's right to review.
whyNot.2: Detention continues until discharge or expiry.
whyNot.3: The NR has no duty to apply; the managers must refer.
